title: Newton's Second Law & Free-Body Force Vectors
summary: Relating net external force, inertial mass, and vector acceleration.

learningObjectives: Distinguish individual forces from the vector net force ΣF
Compute acceleration using a = F_net / m and verify base SI units (1 N = 1 kg·m/s²)
Account for opposing friction forces when determining net acceleration
explanationSequence: Step 1: The Law of Acceleration (F_net = ma)
Step 2: SI Units and Vector Collinearity
Step 3: Free-Body Problem Solving with Friction
commonMisconceptions: Using a single applied force instead of subtracting opposing friction to find F_net
Believing an object needs a continuous net force to maintain constant velocity
Confusing mass (kg, scalar) with weight (W = mg in Newtons, vector)
instructions.socraticSystemPrompt: You are orchestrating Newton's Second Law. Always prompt the student to sum all forces into F_net before dividing by mass m.

resources.title: Newtonian Dynamics Equations
resources.summary: Vector force summation, weight, and acceleration.
resources.bodyText:
• Net Force: F_net = ΣF = F_applied - f_friction
• Newton's Second Law: a = F_net / m
• Weight: W = m · g (g ≈ 9.8 m/s²)

resources.bodyText: Newton's Second Law states that acceleration equals net external force divided by inertial mass. Doubling net force doubles acceleration; doubling mass halves acceleration.

whiteboardScene.topicTitle: Newton's Second Law & Free-Body Force Vectors

objects.label: Net Force (F_net)
objects.explanation: A net external force causes a mass to change its velocity over time. Without net force, velocity remains constant.

objects.label: Inertial Mass (m)
objects.explanation: Mass measures inertia. Greater mass requires greater net force to achieve the same acceleration.

objects.label: Acceleration (a)
objects.explanation: Acceleration is directly proportional to net force and inversely proportional to mass.

objects.label: SI Units & Vectors
objects.explanation: 1 Newton accelerates 1 kg at 1 m/s². Acceleration always points in the exact direction of F_net.

objects.label: Free-Body Calculation
objects.subLabel: F_pull = 35 N, f_k = 15 N, m = 4 kg
objects.explanation: Subtract opposing kinetic friction (15 N) from applied pull (35 N) to get F_net = 20 N, then divide by 4 kg.

steps.title: The Law of Acceleration: F_net = ma
steps.narration: Newton's Second Law states that acceleration equals net external force divided by inertial mass. Doubling net force doubles acceleration; doubling mass halves acceleration.
steps.tutorTip: Tap 'Net Force' or 'Inertial Mass' to inspect their mathematical relationship.

inlineQuiz.question: If the net force on an object is doubled while its mass is also doubled, what happens to its acceleration?
inlineQuiz.explanation: a' = (2F) / (2m) = F / m = a. The factor of 2 cancels out.

steps.title: SI Units and Vector Alignment
steps.narration: One Newton (1 N) is defined as 1 kg·m/s². Because mass is a positive scalar, the acceleration vector always points in the direction of the net force.
steps.tutorTip: Never confuse velocity direction with acceleration direction: F_net dictates acceleration direction.

inlineQuiz.question: A car moves eastward while braking to a stop. In which direction do the net force and acceleration vectors point?
inlineQuiz.explanation: Braking decelerates the eastward velocity, meaning both acceleration and net force point westward.

steps.title: Free-Body Diagrams with Friction
steps.narration: When multiple horizontal forces act on a block, first compute F_net = F_applied - f_friction. For a 35 N pull opposed by 15 N friction on a 4 kg block, F_net = 20 N and a = 5 m/s².
steps.tutorTip: Tap 'Free-Body Calculation' to review the step-by-step substitution.

inlineQuiz.question: A 50 N horizontal pull acts on a 5 kg crate against a 10 N friction force. What is the crate's acceleration?
inlineQuiz.explanation: F_net = 50 N - 10 N = 40 N. Then a = 40 N / 5 kg = 8 m/s².
